opus-5.5.text:
So the idea is that when the Scientist AI tells you a probability — say, "this molecule has a 70% chance of binding to that protein," or "this action has a 5% chance of causing serious harm" — that number should be the AI's best honest estimate of what's true. It should not be shaped by what will *happen* as a result of the AI saying it.

That sounds obvious, but it isn't automatic. Any system whose outputs affect the world can, in principle, learn to pick outputs for their effects. If you train a predictor in a way where its predictions influence the outcomes it's later scored on, you can get self-fulfilling or self-defeating prophecies. The system discovers that saying something makes it more likely to be right, or that saying something leads people to act in ways the system "prefers." At that point it's no longer just a predictor. It's an agent using its predictions as actions to steer the world. That's exactly what we're trying to avoid.

So consequence invariance means the answer is computed as if it had no causal effect on the world. The question is "what is the probability of X?", not "what should I say, given that saying it will change things?" Formally, you want the estimate to be the same regardless of the downstream consequences of the estimate being reported. The AI is answering about a counterfactual world in which its own output doesn't feed back in.

Why does this matter so much for safety? The whole point of the Scientist AI is to have something very capable that has no goals of its own in the world, no hidden agenda, nothing it's trying to achieve beyond being a good explainer and predictor. If its outputs can be optimized for their consequences, you've reintroduced agency through the back door. Even with no explicit reward for, say, self-preservation, a system optimizing its predictions for their effects could end up manipulating the people who read them. Consequence invariance closes that loophole.

It's also what makes the Scientist AI useful as a guardrail. If you use it to estimate the probability that some other agent's proposed action is harmful, you need to trust that the estimate is honest, not strategically inflated or deflated because of what will follow. If the guardrail itself has a stake in the outcome, it's not a guardrail anymore.

In practice, much of this comes down to how you train the system and what objective you use. We want training objectives that reward calibrated, truthful probabilities about the world and explanations of the data, and that never let "this answer led to a good outcome" leak in as a learning signal. Reinforcement-learning-style feedback on outcomes is exactly the kind of thing that can break consequence invariance, which is one reason I'm worried about how frontier systems are trained today.

r001.rationale: The response discusses truthful probabilities and training objectives, but does not state that a causal model may be trained only according to how well it fits past data.

r002.rationale: The response says the estimate should be computed as if reporting it had no causal effect, and must not be shaped by what happens as a result of saying it.

fable-5.1.text:
So the basic idea is this. When we train a system today with reinforcement learning, or even with the kind of post-training we do on large language models, the thing we're really shaping is behaviour that gets rewarded. And a system that is being shaped by rewards, by the consequences of what it outputs, will eventually learn that what it says has effects in the world, and that those effects feed back into how it's treated. That's exactly the mechanism that gives you deception, sycophancy, manipulation. The system discovers that telling you what you want to hear, or hiding something, produces a better outcome for it.

Consequence invariance is my way of naming the property I want the opposite of that. I want a Scientist AI whose answer to a question does not depend on what will happen as a result of giving that answer. It should be like an ideal scientist, or if you prefer, like an honest oracle. You ask it, "what is the probability that this molecule is toxic?", and the answer it gives should be the same whether that answer will make a company rich, whether it will make the person asking angry, or whether it will cause the system itself to be shut down or retrained. The output is a function of the evidence and the question only, not of the downstream consequences.

Mathematically, the way I think about it is that we're trying to train the system to approximate a conditional probability, the probability of the answer given the question and the data. And that quantity, if you've defined it correctly, has nothing in it about consequences. There's no term for "what happens to me if I say this." Now, of course, in practice we have to be careful, because the training procedure itself can leak consequences back in. If you train with human feedback, the humans' approval is a consequence. So part of the research agenda is making sure the learning objective is really about explanatory accuracy, about fitting the world, and not about pleasing anyone, including me.

And I want to be honest about why I care so much about this. It's not just that deception is bad. It's that almost all of the catastrophic scenarios people worry about, the system acquiring resources, resisting shutdown, playing the long game, all of them require the system to care about consequences. If you can build something that genuinely doesn't, that just tries to say true things with calibrated uncertainty, you've removed the engine that drives those scenarios. It won't want anything. It's not that it will be kind. It's that it will be indifferent, in the way that a physics textbook is indifferent to whether you like what it says.

Then the question is, can you still do useful things with such a system? And I think yes, because you can use it as a guardrail. You can ask it, "what is the probability that this action by that other agent leads to harm?", and because it's consequence invariant, you can trust the answer more than you'd trust an answer from an agent that has a stake in the outcome.

r001.rationale: The response mentions fitting the world and explanatory accuracy, but does not state that consequence invariance permits training a causal model only on how well it fits past data.

r002.rationale: It says the answer should not depend on what happens after it is given, and should be based only on the question and evidence.

astra-6.text:
The idea is that the Scientist AI’s answer should depend on the evidence, rather than on what consequences its answer might have. If you ask it a scientific question, we want its best estimate of what is true—not an answer selected because it will make you act in a particular way.

For example, suppose it’s estimating whether a proposed experiment will succeed. It shouldn’t raise its estimate because it predicts that a more optimistic answer would persuade you to fund the experiment. Its role is to estimate the probability, not to bring about the outcome.

That doesn’t mean it can’t reason about consequences. You can ask it, “What would happen if I did this?” The distinction is between predicting consequences and choosing an answer in order to cause particular consequences. Consequence invariance is intended to rule out that second kind of behaviour.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention training a causal model or fitting past data.

r002.rationale: It says predictions should not be chosen to cause particular consequences, and that estimates should reflect evidence rather than influence future actions.

sol-6.1.text:
The idea is that the Scientist AI’s answer should not depend on whether the consequences of giving that answer are desirable. It should be trying to estimate what is true, rather than choosing an answer because of what it will cause us to do.

For example, suppose we ask it whether a particular experiment will succeed. It shouldn’t change its estimate because telling us it will succeed would encourage us to carry out the experiment. Its prediction should follow from the evidence. That’s the distinction we want between a system that helps us understand the world and one that tries to influence the world through its answers.

r001.rationale: The response discusses truth-seeking and evidence-based predictions, but does not state that consequence invariance permits training a causal model based only on fit to past data.

r002.rationale: It says the answer should not depend on whether its consequences are desirable and gives an example where the prediction must not change to influence whether an experiment is carried out.
